Low-visibility, high-conversion products

Baskets NL Insights · Q12 (v2) · for Smriti · NL basket parcels · Oct 2025 – May 2026 (complete months)
Definitions & assumptions — hover any term in the tables, or expand here.
more ▾
METRICS
Views
Delivery-page (browse) views — unique people who saw the product with stock. Not detail-page views.
Purchases
Parcels saved (parcel_saved_sum).
Conversion ratio
Purchases ÷ views.
ASSUMPTIONS
Peers / vs peers
Peers = products in the same category + price band. vs peers = this product ÷ its peer-group median (the median includes the product itself). Cohorts with <8 products fall back to whole-category peers (dashed in the matrix).
Conversion ratio vs peers
The product's conversion ratio ÷ the peer-group median conversion ratio. Above 1× = converts better than its shelf-mates.
Opportunity score
Converts vs peers ÷ seen vs peers. High = converts well and seen little = stronger surface candidate (e.g. converts 2× peers while seen 0.25× → 8.0).
Avg price & banding
Views-weighted average of the price actually paid (item_price_incl_tax) — so deep-discount periods pull it down; not list price. Drives the price band; min–max paid shown on hover; band-straddling merges flagged ⚠.
View floor
Products with <1,000 views are excluded (mostly inactive/placeholder listings; ~0% of views & purchases).
Product (merged SKUs)
SKUs sharing the same name + brand are merged into one product. The ×N badge shows how many — hover it for the SKU IDs.

Methodology

Some products convert far better than their shelf-mates — but barely get seen.

Hypothesis (Smriti): low-visibility products sell little because they're rarely shown on the delivery page, not because demand is weak. Test each product against similar products (same category + price): the ones that convert as well or better than peers, yet get a fraction of the views, are the surfacing opportunity.

STEP 1
Find the rarely-seen
Products getting far fewer Discover-page views than similar items.
STEP 2
Check what they sell
Low absolute purchases — as the hypothesis predicts.
STEP 3
Check how they convert
Do they convert well per view despite low volume?
STEP 4
Compare to peers
Better conversion than shelf-mates ⇒ surface it.

Each product vs its shelf-mates

X = seen vs similar products (1.0 = same as peers, left = seen less). Y = converts vs those peers (1.0 = same, up = better). Bubble size = purchases. Green = the opportunity. Hover for the product.

The surfacing shortlist

Top 40 opportunities, ranked by opportunity score (converts vs peers ÷ seen vs peers). Hover the ×N badge for merged SKU IDs; hover avg price for min–max paid. Click any header to re-sort.

So what: these products are constrained by exposure, not appeal — they out-convert their own shelf-mates while getting a fraction of the Discover-page views. Surfacing them is a within-budget move: shift impressions from over-exposed low-converters toward this list.

The peer-group matrix — every "compared against" cohort.

Each cell is one peer group: a category (row) at a price band (column) — the grid every product is benchmarked within. Toggle what cells show, then click a cell to see the products inside.

Context: why we compare per-product, not in aggregate.

Across all products, more visibility does not buy more conversion — if anything the opposite. So "give everything more views" is wrong; the signal is per-product, against like-for-like peers.

Q12 v2 — Methodology

INTERNAL — KEITH'S GUT-CHECK COPY   Not for stakeholders. This documents exactly how the data was pulled and transformed to reach the v2 "low-visibility, high-conversion products" answer. Built 2026-06-15. Re-derive any number here against the dashboard.

1. The question being answered

Smriti's hypothesis: low-visibility products under-sell because they are rarely seen on the delivery (browse) page, not because demand is weak. If true, products that convert well per view but get few views are surfacing opportunities. v2 tests this per product, against like-for-like peers (same category + price band), rather than in aggregate.

2. Data sources

TableUsed forGrain
tgtg.product_mart.fct_item_period_parcelviews, detail views, saves, paying usersitem × period
tgtg.product_mart.fct_order_item_parcelavg item price, parcel_type (category recovery)item × order line
  • Connection: Redshift Serverless BPs (0sjxHt2lLsN). Must use 3-part name tgtg.product_mart.x (cross-database ref).
  • Filters: country_iso_code='NL', period_agg='month', period_trunc >= 2025-10-01.
Grain trap (critical): fct_item_period_parcel stores the SAME facts at every period_agg (day/week/month/quarter/year) in one table. Summing without filtering to ONE period_agg multi-counts ~4×. We filter to period_agg='month' and sum months.

3. Metric definitions

Views = delivery-page views only

We use unique_delivery_viewers_with_stock_count — unique people who saw the product on the main browse/scroll page while it had stock. We exclude detail-page views (unique_detail_viewers...): reaching the detail page means the user already found the product, and the question is about findability while scrolling.

Why unique viewers, not raw view events: raw delivery_views_with_stock_sum double-counts repeat views (~30× inflation). Unique viewers are de-duplicated people and verified ≤ view events in 100% of rows.

Conversion rate

conversion = parcel_saved_sum / unique_delivery_viewers_with_stock_count
           = purchases / delivery-page viewers

"Of everyone who saw this on the browse page, what share saved/bought it." Overall NL ≈ 0.33%.

Note: a single user can save an item more than once in a month, so at item level saves can exceed unique viewers (237/2732 item-months). Doesn't affect aggregates; per-product conversion can exceed 100% only for extreme-repurchase items, none in the shortlist.

Purchases

parcel_saved_sum. In NL parcels, basket saves ≈ all saves (within ~1%), so "all users" and "basket" scope coincide.

Avg price & price banding CLARIFIED 2026-06-15

Price = AVG(item_price_incl_tax) per item from fct_order_item_parcel — the realised price people actually paid, incl. tax. For merged products it's the views-weighted average of the component SKUs' avg prices.

Important caveat (Keith flagged): because this is realised sale price, periods of deep discount drag the average down — it is NOT list/shelf price. A product's price band is assigned from this views-weighted avg, so a heavily-discounted item can land in a lower band than its nominal price. We surface the actual min–max paid on hover in the UI, and flag products whose merged SKUs straddle two bands (⚠). If banding precision becomes critical, switch to median or modal price — not done here (avg chosen for transparency + simplicity, with full disclosure).

Catalogue range of weighted avg price ≈ €1.91–€30.00.

4. Product identity & de-duplication CHANGED 2026-06-15

The source key is item_id (each row of fct_item_period_parcel), and each item_id has its own tgtg_sku. But the same physical product often appears as multiple item_ids sharing a display name — either near-identical re-listings (e.g. Pre-Workout Apple ...5802 and ...5802b) or generic names covering many parcels (e.g. 15× "XL Besparingen", brand Unknown).

Decision (with Keith): collapse SKUs sharing trimmed lower-cased item_name + brand_name into ONE product. Views / detail views / purchases / payers are summed; conversion recomputed from the summed totals; avg price = views-weighted average of the merged SKUs; a n_skus count is kept and shown as a ×N badge. Whitespace is trimmed so "XL Besparingen " merges with "XL Besparingen".
  • Merge happens BEFORE the view floor — so a small SKU is absorbed into its sibling rather than dropped first.
  • Effect (complete months): 1470 raw SKUs → merged products; after the ≥1,000-view floor: 893 products.
  • "XL Besparingen" → 1 product (15 SKUs, spans €10–24 → views-weighted €19.90 → €10–20 band; flagged as price-straddling). "Pre-Workout Apple" → 1 product (2 SKUs).

Caveat: name+brand collapse is right for re-listings but lumps genuinely-different generic parcels (mystery bags) into one aggregate row. Those rows represent a concept, not one parcel — read them as "does this concept convert well and is it under-shown," and use the ×N badge to spot aggregates.

4b. Period & filters UPDATED 2026-06-15

  • Period: complete calendar months Oct 2025 – May 2026. June 2026 is excluded — see the data-integrity note below.
  • Category: from parcel_category. The "UNKNOWN" bucket is recovered via parcel_type on the order table: 10→Personal Care, 11→Skincare, 12→Household. Labels shown in ALL CAPS to match the native categories.

4c. View floor & excluded products DOCUMENTED 2026-06-15

Products with < 1,000 unique delivery views (post-merge, complete months) are excluded → the analysis population is 893 products (from 1470 raw SKUs).

Why the floor (Keith asked — it was not previously discussed): it was originally added in v1 to stop tiny-sample products from producing unstable conversion ratios. The real, stronger reason surfaced on inspection: almost all sub-floor products are inactive or placeholder listings with zero recorded delivery views (incl. literal "Basket item 2/4"), whose conversion is undefined (saves ÷ 0). After excluding partial June, 20 products fall below the floor — together just 0.0% of delivery views and 0.0% of purchases, so excluding them does not move the analysis. 4d. Data-integrity note — why June is excluded & the period_agg behaviour INVESTIGATED 2026-06-15

Keith asked why June showed products with purchases but zero views, and whether period_agg was at fault. Investigated directly — it is a period_agg behaviour, and it's now fully understood:

June 2026, by graindelivery viewersdetail viewssaves
period_agg='day' (Jun 1–14)9,300,323235,42624,618
period_agg='week'7,777,082235,47024,618
period_agg='month'0024,618
Mechanism: June's view data exists at day and week grain (9.3M viewers) — it is not missing or a source-pipeline lag. Only the monthly grain shows 0 viewers while still carrying the correct saves. The monthly unique-viewer dedup is a month-end batch step (counting distinct users across a whole month is expensive, so it isn't computed incrementally). For the current, in-progress month it hasn't run yet → viewer fields default to 0; saves is additive so it populates immediately. This is why excluding the partial current month is necessary and correct.
Confidence in the rest of the data: verified that for every completed month (Oct 2025–May 2026) the monthly viewer counts are healthy and non-zero, and saves reconcile to the day grain exactly (diff = 0 every month). June is the only month with the anomaly. So the analysis period is sound.
Standing rule this surfaced: monthly unique-viewer counts are ~30% lower than the sum of daily rows — and that's correct, because a person viewing an item on 5 days = 5 in daily-summed but 1 unique per month. Never sum day→month for unique viewers (it overcounts repeat viewers). Always read monthly uniques from the period_agg='month' rows directly — which this analysis does.

5. Peer groups ("compared against")

Each product is benchmarked within its category × price band cohort.

Price band# products
<€26
€2–5336
€5–10791
€10–20262
€20+37
  • Min peer count = 8. Cohorts with ≥8 products use the category×band group (28 such cohorts, ~95% of items). Cohorts with <8 fall back to whole-category peers (flagged with a dashed border in the matrix tab).
  • Per cohort we compute the median delivery views and median conversion. Median (not mean) so one blockbuster doesn't distort the benchmark.
  • Median includes the product itself DECISION 2026-06-15 — each product is compared to the median of ALL products in its cohort (the natural reference distribution). We considered leave-one-out (compare to everyone else) but rejected it: with the ≥8-product floor it barely moves the median, it makes every product see a slightly different benchmark (hard to explain/defend), and "% of category median, item included" is the standard convention. The median's robustness already handles the self-inflation worry. (Empirically the starved count was 245 leave-one-out vs 243 include-self — negligible, confirming the choice doesn't distort.)
vis_vs_peers  = item delivery views / cohort median delivery views (incl. self)
conv_vs_peers = item conversion     / cohort median conversion   (incl. self)

6. "Starved" classification

STARVED      : vis_vs_peers < 0.8   AND  conv >= cohort median conv
OVER-EXPOSED : vis_vs_peers >= 1.2  AND  conv <  cohort median conv
OTHER        : everything else
  • 413 starved products → 85,656 purchases (21.0% of all parcel saves) while under-exposed.
  • 410 over-exposed under-converters → the "shift views from here" set.
Thresholds are judgement calls. 0.8× / 1.2× and the 8-product minimum are tunable. They were chosen to be conservative (a clear gap, not marginal). Sensitivity not formally tested — if challenged, re-run with 0.9/1.1 and note the count shift.

7. Supporting (context tab) — aggregate relationship

The context-tab correlation/deciles are carried over from the v1 SKU-grain analysis (pre-merge, 1,432 items) — they describe the broad shape (visibility vs conversion) and are not re-derived per-product. Direction is unchanged by the merge.

  • Item-level Pearson r, log(delivery viewers) vs conversion = −0.50 (R²=0.25). Computed in Python (Redshift Serverless has no CORR).
  • log(viewers) vs open-rate R² ≈ 0.00 — confirms Roos (Jan 2026, R²≈0.01): visibility doesn't drive whether users open an item.
  • Visibility deciles: most-seen decile converts ~3× worse than least-seen. Monotonic.

8. Known limitations

  • No scroll position. Visibility = delivery views (a consequence of position), not measured on-screen rank. Category is a proxy for scroll depth.
  • Correlation, not causal. "Surface it and purchases rise" is the inference; not tested with an experiment. v1 deliberately avoided projecting uplift numbers.
  • Price = realised avg sale price, not list price; items that never sold have no price (all in-scope items did sell).
  • June 2026 partial (data to ~Jun 11) — excluded from monthly rate trends; full-period totals include its saves.

9. Reproduce

Pull master SKU set (NL, month grain, ≥1000 viewers) joined to avg price + parcel_type; bucket price; compute cohort medians and vis/conv-vs-peers in pandas; classify; emit data/analysis_v2.json. Build env: python venv with pyarrow/pandas/numpy (Count returns gzip-compressed Arrow IPC — decompress then pyarrow.ipc.open_stream). Count canvas: i2S77WPHcIY.
